h1: Sweetness, acidity and tannin in wine
title: Sweetness, Acidity and Tannin in Wine | Craft Beer School
desc: What sweetness, acidity and tannin mean in wine, where each comes from and how they shape taste, food pairing and complaints.
teaser: Most arguments about whether a wine is good are really arguments about three things you can measure.
standfirst: Ask ten people to describe a wine and you get ten answers. Ask them about sweetness, acidity and tannin and they start to agree. This guide explains the structure of a wine for people who work with it but have never made it.
sections: Wine people separate flavour from structure. Flavour is the fruit, spice or oak you smell. Structure is what the wine does in your mouth: how sweet it is, how sharp, how drying. Structure is easier to measure, easier to agree on and often the real cause when a customer says a wine is "wrong". Our guide to wine tasting for beginners covers the flavour side.

Grapes are full of sugar. Yeast turns that sugar into alcohol. Whatever sugar the yeast does not convert stays in the wine as residual sugar, measured in grams per litre.

Most table wines are dry, with only a few grams per litre that the tongue barely notices. Off-dry wines carry a little more. Dessert wines can carry well over a hundred grams. A winemaker can stop fermentation early by chilling the wine or removing the yeast, which leaves sweetness behind.

Two traps for newcomers. First, ripe fruit aromas can make a dry wine seem sweet. Second, acidity hides sugar, so a wine with plenty of both can taste less sweet than its lab number suggests.

Acidity is what makes your mouth water. Grapes contain mainly tartaric and malic acid. Many red wines and some whites go through a second, bacterial conversion that turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid. That is why some Chardonnay tastes buttery and round rather than crisp.

Winemakers track acidity as titratable acidity and as pH. Most wines fall somewhere between about pH 3 and 4. A lower pH tastes sharper, protects the wine better against spoilage and helps it age.

Climate drives a lot of this. Grapes lose acid quickly as they ripen in heat. Indian vineyards, with warm days and harvests in the cooler early months of the year, have to manage that carefully. Winemakers may pick earlier or adjust acidity in the winery. Read about Indian wine regions for the growing conditions.

Tannin is the drying, gripping feeling a strong cup of black tea leaves on your gums. It comes from grape skins, seeds and stems. Oak barrels add more. Tannin binds to proteins in saliva, which is why the mouth feels rough.

Red wines are high in tannin because they ferment with their skins, which also give them their colour. White wines are pressed off the skins early, so they have very little. Thick-skinned grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah bring more tannin than thin-skinned Pinot Noir. Tannin softens over years in bottle, one reason big reds are often aged before drinking.

None of this is left to chance. In the vineyard, the picking date sets the balance between sugar and acid: earlier fruit is sharper and lighter, later fruit riper and lower in acid. In the winery, the length of skin contact sets how much tannin and colour a red extracts. Oak ageing adds tannin of its own. Stopping fermentation early, or blending in a little sweet grape juice where the rules allow, leaves sweetness behind.

The lab checks each of these before bottling: residual sugar, titratable acidity, pH and alcohol. The tasting team then judges whether the numbers add up to the wine the label promises. When a vintage comes in unbalanced, those are the levers the winemaker pulls.

A good wine keeps the three in proportion with its alcohol and fruit. Too much acid with too little fruit tastes thin. Too much tannin with too little fruit tastes harsh. Sweetness without acidity tastes flabby.

The same logic drives food pairing. Tannin softens against fat and protein, so a firm red suits a rich mutton curry or a kebab platter. High acidity cuts through cream and butter, which helps with a butter chicken or a malai kofta. Chilli heat makes tannin and alcohol feel harsher, while a touch of sweetness calms it, so an off-dry white is often the easiest match for a fiery Andhra or Chettinad dish. These are suggestions, not rules.
Why it matters at your desk

Spec sheets, product copy and customer complaints all use this language. When someone writes that a wine is "too sour" they usually mean high acidity. "Bitter" often means tannin. "Too sweet" may be fruit and oak rather than sugar. A team that can tell these apart writes better descriptions, handles complaints faster and asks the winery better questions.

A short guided tasting of three contrasting wines teaches this quickly. Keep it opt-in and within company policy, with spit cups and non-drinkers welcome to smell and take notes.
faqs: What is residual sugar in wine?
The grape sugar left after fermentation, measured in grams per litre. Dry wines have only a few grams, dessert wines far more.
Why do red wines feel drying?
Tannin from the grape skins, seeds and oak binds to proteins in saliva. Reds ferment with their skins, so they carry much more tannin than whites.
Can a dry wine taste sweet?
Yes. Ripe fruit aromas and alcohol can give an impression of sweetness even when residual sugar is very low.
What wine suits spicy Indian food?
Off-dry whites with good acidity are often the easiest match, because a little sweetness calms chilli heat. High tannin reds tend to clash with heavy spice.
